terms.meaning: The 2025 edition of OWASP's awareness list of the ten most critical web application security risks.
#1 risk in OWASP Top 10:2025, keeping the top spot it first took in 2021.
Systems, applications or cloud services configured insecurely; A02 in OWASP Top 10:2025, up from #5 in 2021.
A03 in OWASP Top 10:2025: compromises anywhere in the software supply chain; broadens 2021's outdated-components risk.
Risks from missing or ineffective security design rather than implementation bugs; introduced in 2021.
New in Top 10:2025: improper error handling, logical errors, failing open and related scenarios.
2021's 'Security Logging and Monitoring Failures' renamed 'Security Logging and Alerting Failures' in 2025.
Retired 2021 category; expanded into A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures.
Application Security Verification Standard: about 350 requirements in 17 chapters; released May 30, 2025.
4.0.3 is superseded by 5.0.0; a two-way v4.0/v5.0 mapping is provided to ease migration.
ASVS levels: L1 first layer of defense, L2 standard security practices, L3 advanced high-assurance.
OWASP maturity model for software security programs: 5 business functions, 15 security practices, 3 maturity levels.
MITRE ranking of the most dangerous software weaknesses, released Dec 11, 2025; CWE view 1435.
Writes data past the end, or before the start, of the intended buffer; #5 on the 2025 CWE Top 25.
Memory is reused or referenced after it has been freed; #7 on the 2025 CWE Top 25.
Input is not validated, or is validated incorrectly, before it is processed; #18 on the 2025 Top 25.
Product contains hard-coded credentials. Children: CWE-259 hard-coded password, CWE-321 hard-coded key.
Deserializing untrusted data into objects, which can run attacker code or forge application state.
Untrusted input written to logs without neutralization, so an attacker can forge or split entries.
Sensitive data kept unencrypted at rest, readable by anyone who reaches the store or its copies.
CWE class for design-principle violations; parent of CWE-250, CWE-636, CWE-638, CWE-656 and more.
On error or failure, the design falls back to a less secure state than others available. Child of CWE-657.
Protection whose strength depends mainly on its obscurity; knowing how it works defeats it. Child of CWE-657.
'Dependency on Vulnerable Third-Party Component': a dependency has one or more known vulnerabilities.
A weakness type (CWE) vs one published vulnerability instance (CVE): the classic lookalike mix-up.
Software development life cycle with security activities built into every phase, requirements to release.
Security Development Lifecycle; an integral part of Microsoft's development process since 2004.
NIST Secure Software Development Framework: secure development practices in four groups; v1.1 published Feb 2022.
SSDF groups: Prepare the Organization, Protect the Software, Produce Well-Secured Software, Respond to Vulnerabilities.

spec.as: NIST SSDF · PO · PS · PW · RV

terms.meaning: SSDF 1.1: 'Verify Third-Party Software Complies with Security Requirements' was moved to PW.4.
'Security Considerations in the SDLC' withdrawn May 31, 2019; NIST points to SP 800-160 Vol. 1.
US order 'Improving the Nation's Cybersecurity' (May 12, 2021); drove NIST's SSDF and SBOM guidance.
EU Cyber Resilience Act: reporting duties from 11 Sep 2026, main obligations from 11 Dec 2027.
Structured analysis of a system to find what can go wrong and decide what to do about it.
Threat-classification mnemonic: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, DoS, Elevation of privilege.
Legacy threat risk-rating mnemonic: Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, Discoverability.
Privacy threat types: Linking, Identifying, Non-repudiation, Detecting, Data Disclosure, Unawareness, Non-compliance.
Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis: a seven-stage, risk-centric threat modeling method.
Second of the four key questions in the Threat Modeling Manifesto.
Threat Modeling Manifesto anti-pattern: depending on one gifted person instead of a shared practice.
Model of processes, data stores, external entities and data flows; the usual base for a threat model.
Line in a system model where trust level changes; threats cluster where data flows cross it.
All the points where an attacker can try to enter data into or extract data from a system.
Scenario describing how a feature could be misused, written alongside ordinary use cases.
Microsoft's threat modeling card game, with suits based on the STRIDE categories.
Each account and process gets only the privileges it needs; CWE-250 'Execution with Unnecessary Privileges' violates it.
Products ship with secure settings already on; SSDF PW.9: 'Configure Software to Have Secure Settings by Default'.
Design principle that protection stays simple; CWE-637 'Unnecessary Complexity in Protection Mechanism' violates it.
Static Application Security Testing: analyzes source code or binaries without running them.
Dynamic Application Security Testing: probes a running application from the outside.
Software Composition Analysis: inventories third-party components and flags known vulnerabilities.
Interactive Application Security Testing: instruments the running app to observe flaws during tests.
Feeding generated or malformed inputs to find crashes and bugs; also an OpenSSF Scorecard check.
Taint-analysis model: untrusted data from a source must be sanitized before it reaches a sensitive sink.
SCA technique that checks whether vulnerable code in a dependency is actually called by the app.
Static Analysis Results Interchange Format; OASIS Standard since March 27, 2020.
GitHub's semantic code analysis engine: it builds a database of the code and runs QL queries against it.
Pattern-based static analysis tool whose rules look like the code they match.
DAST tool that left OWASP in Sep 2023; known as 'ZAP by Checkmarx' since Sep 24, 2024; still open source.
Software Bill of Materials: a nested inventory of the components that make up a piece of software.
OWASP bill-of-materials standard, also standardized by Ecma as ECMA-424.
Linux Foundation SBOM standard; 3.0 reorganized the model into profiles. SPDX 2.2.1 is ISO/IEC 5962:2021.
Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange: states whether a product is affected by a given vulnerability.
VEX status: no remediation required; must say why, via a justification label or an impact statement.
VEX justification: the vulnerable code is present but is not called or used by the product.
Package-URL: ecosystem-neutral package identifier; ECMA-427 1st edition published December 2025.
Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: graded levels of supply chain integrity, starting with the build.
v1.0 kept v0.1's Level 1–3 build and provenance requirements, deferring Level 4 and source requirements.
Sigstore trio: signing client, code-signing certificate authority, append-only transparency log.
Automated checks such as Pinned-Dependencies and Token-Permissions that score a project's security habits.
Renamed from 'CII Best Practices badge' on 2021-12-24; the Scorecard check is still CII-Best-Practices.
CISA-led 2026 Minimum Elements (Jul 29, 2026) update and replace NTIA's 2021 SBOM minimum elements.
Critical Apache Log4j 2 flaw disclosed Dec 2021; the defining case for SCA and SBOM programs.
Backdoor found in xz release tarballs in March 2024; a landmark open source supply chain case.
Tiny npm package whose March 2016 removal broke builds worldwide; a lesson in dependency fragility.
Practice of moving security activities earlier in the life cycle, closer to design and coding.
Developer embedded in a team who advocates for and coordinates security work.
Well-supported default tooling and patterns that make the secure path the easy path.
SDL severity criteria for rating security bugs and setting the minimum quality bar for release.
Triage outcome: the finding is real, but its owner formally accepts the residual risk.
Bandit inline comment that suppresses findings on a line; can name specific test IDs.
GitHub Actions line that disables all GITHUB_TOKEN permissions; grant back only what a job needs.
Scanner summary line a release gate hopes to read before shipping.
First of the four key questions in the Threat Modeling Manifesto; model the system before asking what can go wrong.
Principle 1 in Viega and McGraw's Building Secure Software: a system is only as strong as its weakest component.
First of OWASP's Security by Design Principles: every feature adds risk, so keep the exposed surface small.
Principle 9 in Viega and McGraw's Building Secure Software: assume a hostile environment and give trust sparingly.
Saltzer and Schroeder's 1975 principle: minimize the mechanism shared by more than one user and relied on by all.

terms.text: Grant only what the job needs
terms.meaning: Least privilege: every account and process gets the minimum access its task requires, and no more.

spec.as: Grant the least privilege that still lets the job run.

terms.meaning: When a check cannot decide, because of an error or missing data, the safe answer is deny; CWE-636 is the opposite.

spec.as: When a check cannot decide, the answer must be no.

terms.meaning: Data is checked where it crosses each trust boundary, not once at the perimeter.

spec.as: Validate at every trust boundary, not once at the edge.

terms.meaning: NVD placeholder: the weakness is not covered by the subset of CWE that NVD maps to.
SARIF result kind: the rule was not evaluated because it does not apply to the analysis target.
Latin a and Cyrillic a look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable, so names can be spoofed.
Latin e and Cyrillic ie look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Latin o and Cyrillic o look the same in most fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Lowercase Latin l and capital I look the same in many sans-serif fonts; Unicode UTS #39 lists them as confusable.
Known-answer test: 8-digit TOTP with HMAC-SHA-1, the RFC 6238 Appendix B key and Unix time 1111111109.
Known-answer test: 6-digit HOTP for counter 0 with the RFC 4226 Appendix D key.
Known-answer test: PBKDF2 of "password" with salt "salt", one iteration and a 20-byte key; first 32 bits shown.
NVD placeholder: the advisory gave too little information to assign a weakness.
Insufficient Logging: security-critical events go unrecorded or lack key details, leaving forensics blind.
OWASP Top 10:2025 category for weak, missing or misused cryptography; down from #2 in 2021.
OWASP moved Cryptographic Failures from #2 (2021) to #4 (2025); in 2017 it was Sensitive Data Exposure.
OWASP Top 10:2025 category covering XSS and SQL injection among 37 mapped CWEs.
SSRF lost its own Top 10 slot and was rolled into Broken Access Control.
Vulnerable and Outdated Components grew into Software Supply Chain Failures.
XSS lost its own slot in 2021 and joined Injection (now A05:2025).
Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource: the weakness behind world-readable storage.
Initialization of a Resource with an Insecure Default: open-by-default services and settings.
Obsolete CWE category, mapping prohibited; map the real weakness, e.g. a descendant of CWE-284.
Improper Certificate Validation; MASWE-0027 (validation) and MASWE-0028 (pinning) map to it.
Cleartext Transmission of Sensitive Information: the usual class for unencrypted-protocol findings.
Weakness behind the classic default-password finding; added to CWE in October 2022.
A07 in OWASP Top 10:2025: flaws in proving who a user is; was 'Identification and Authentication Failures'.
A08 in OWASP Top 10:2025: failing to verify the integrity of code and data; was 'Software and Data Integrity Failures'.
Building Security In Maturity Model: a descriptive survey of the software security practices real firms run.
OWASP's catalog of ten defensive controls developers build into their code to avoid common security issues.
Practice of building security into every stage of DevOps delivery, with automated checks inside the pipeline.
Supply chain attack where a build fetches a public package named like an internal one; Alex Birsan, 2021.
Public statement of threat modeling's values, principles and anti-patterns, written by a working group of practitioners.
Tree diagram with an attacker's goal at the root and the ways to reach it as branches; popularized by Schneier in 1999.
The documented secure setting for every security-relevant option, so defaults start safe; SSDF PW.9.1.
Refuse every request unless it is explicitly authorized; the access strategy of SP 800-53 SA-8(23) Secure Defaults.
Default settings kept in a usable, versioned format under change control; an SSDF PW.9.2 example.
Force the administrator to replace each default credential during installation; a CWE-1392 mitigation.
Login that needs two or more independent factors; secure-by-default guidance makes it opt-out for admins.
CWE class: the product uses weak credentials; parent of CWE-1392 default and CWE-798 hard-coded credentials.
VEX status: not yet known whether the product versions are affected; later VEX documents update it.
SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control Secure Defaults: a system's as-shipped configuration enforces its security policy.
SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control Secure Failure and Recovery: neither a failure nor its recovery may break security policy.
SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control System Documentation: admin and user guides, secure configuration included.
SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control Configuration Settings: the most restrictive mode consistent with operations.
